Analysis: How Long Can the NFA Injunction Last? [Member Exclusive]

  • Stephen Gutowski
  • October 4, 2026
  • 5:04 am
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:28
Instaread

We found out this week that the Department of Justice (DOJ) has officially decided against appealing the decision in Silencer Shop v. ATF. Does that mean much of the National Firearms Act (NFA) will stay blocked forever?

On Thursday, a letter from Solicitor General John Sauer to the Senate Judiciary Committee was made public and revealed the Department had made its final decision on the case. He said DOJ will not appeal the ruling. But while he briefly outlined the details of the decision, he did not elaborate on the reasoning behind the Department’s choice.

Nonetheless, the choice makes the injunction against most NFA regulations on silencers, short-barrel shotguns and rifles, and any other weapons more permanent. Still, it’s unclear how long that might last, and some risks remain in the short term.

The injunction is a big deal. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) has already told gun dealers they can transfer affected NFA items on a basic background check for circumstances where the injunction applies. Figuring out exactly what circumstances those are remains a mess, but the injunction’s impact is clearly very expansive, and the ATF has promised to release further guidance on how far it believes the coverage extends.

However, the injunction is not unlimited, nor is it necessarily permanent.

It’s brittle for a number of reasons. Advocates didn’t have the votes to actually repeal the NFA, which meant they went a different route and cut the taxes that underlie it to $0 through the bare-majority vote required by reconciliation. The move was designed to undermine the NFA’s constitutionality by attacking the taxing-power argument it has relied on since its passage in 1934.

Gun-rights advocates then sued in a favorable circuit, got a favorable district judge, and convinced him the tax cut did, indeed, unsettle the NFA’s constitutional footing. Then they managed to convince the Trump Administration, and at least according to CBS News President Donald Trump himself, that DOJ shouldn’t appeal the decision.

So, the legal fight is probably done for the moment. Perhaps the gun-control groups or Democratic state Attorneys General will sue to try and force the DOJ to appeal the decision, but that seems unlikely to work. So long as the tax cuts remain and the Trump Administration controls the DOJ, the injunction will probably stand.

This was probably the best strategy available given a proper repeal effort likely wouldn’t have reached the 60-vote threshold to overcome the Senate filibuster. And it worked. Again, at least for the moment.

But the path to victory for gun-rights activists in this case could be fairly easily replicated by gun-control activists. The NFA isn’t completely gone. A large chunk of it is momentarily enjoined, but nobody can know how long the moment will last or what exactly might happen if it is overturned.

Two years seems like a decent bet for the minimum time the state of play remains frozen, since that’s the earliest you are likely to see a new Democratic administration that could order the DOJ to begin trying to enforce the NFA again. But it is actually possible things could change earlier than that. Polling indicates Democrats have a real chance of capturing both the House and Senate.

If Democrats control the reconciliation process next year, they may push to undo the NFA tax cuts in the next omnibus budget. Some top Democrats, including Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy, have already floated raising it into the thousands. But even just crafting a deal to put the tax back to $200 or a single dollar could restore the tax-power justification for the NFA.

It’s not clear what happens to the people and businesses currently covered by the injunction in a scenario where the NFA comes back. It’s possible, perhaps even likely, that a judge undoing the current ruling will provide legal cover for people who bought under the good-faith understanding that the injunction protected them. But who knows for sure?

It’s also possible that all the silencers and short-barrel rifles sold in the next few months to years change the political calculus of reimposing NFA restrictions. Or, at least, doing so without a carveout for people who bought under the injunction. Gun politics only seems to have polarized further in recent years. So, who knows for sure?

Still, regardless of the uncertainty around the injunction’s future, we at least know it’ll be around for a while longer–probably years.
